_note: Sensing-truck scenario: an autonomous digging robot at the Moon's south pole. NO real-world dataset covers these sensors in these conditions, so most numbers are ILLUSTRATIVE placeholders. The exceptions are marked 'sourced' in each sensor's detect_basis, with the evidence listed under 'evidence'. The ordering (radar most robust in dust, lidar and cameras hurt by dust, cameras blind in the dark) is supported by the evidence; the exact percentages are not. Headlights have no detection of their own; their boosts replace a camera's value in shadow and dark when both are fitted.
title: Can the truck see?
intro: NASA's Artemis plans need robots that drive and dig on their own near the Moon's south pole, like NASA's IPEx excavator. There, the Sun stays 1 to 2 degrees above the horizon, so shadows are long and some craters never see sunlight. Pick sensors so the truck spots rocks in every condition, then drive it.
lesson: Each sensor fails in a different place, so a good set covers each other's weak spots within mass, power and budget. NASA's VIPER rover is designed with headlights for exactly this reason: cameras need light in the shadows.
fusion_note: Coverage words come from a simple model: sensors are treated as independent, and most of their numbers are illustrative (hover a word to see the model value). Only the structured-light 97% is a measured NASA figure.

conditions.name: Dust from digging
conditions.why: Digging throws up dust that scatters laser light and blurs cameras. Radar still sees through it, but with less detail.

conditions.name: Long shadows (Sun 1-2° high)
conditions.why: Rocks hide in long black shadows, so cameras struggle. Lidar and headlights bring their own light.

conditions.name: Crater that never sees sunlight
conditions.why: Permanently dark. Cameras need headlights; lidar and radar do not need light.

conditions.name: Crater rim slope
conditions.why: The truck tilts, so sensors point at the sky or the ground instead of ahead.

sensors.name: Camera
sensors.blurb: Cheap and light, but needs light and clean air.
sensors.basis_note: Illustrative numbers. Only the direction is supported by evidence: cameras struggle in dark shadows and lose detail in dust.

sensors.name: Stereo camera
sensors.blurb: Depth from two cameras. Same weak spots as one.
sensors.basis_note: Illustrative numbers. Only the direction is supported by evidence: stereo imaging is 'promising' for polar rovers in NASA Ames early results, but still needs light.

sensors.name: LED headlights
sensors.blurb: Light for the cameras in shadow and darkness, like NASA's VIPER rover.
sensors.basis_note: Headlights see nothing on their own; they let the cameras work in the dark. The idea is real (VIPER is designed as the first lunar rover with headlights, tuned for permanently shadowed regions); the improvement numbers are illustrative.

sensors.name: Lidar
sensors.blurb: Laser scanner: great in dark and shadow, hurt by dust.
sensors.basis_note: Illustrative numbers. Only the direction is supported by evidence: lidar performance degrades in dust.

sensors.name: Radar
sensors.blurb: Sees through dust and dark, but only coarse shapes.
sensors.basis_note: Illustrative numbers. Only the direction is supported by evidence: radar sees through dust with relatively low loss, but is coarse.

sensors.name: Structured-light bumper
sensors.blurb: A laser-dot pattern read by a camera. Tested by NASA Ames.
sensors.basis_note: About 97% obstacle detection in NASA Ames K-REX2 tests lit like direct sunlight and like shadowed craters (day and night image sets). Dust and slope are not covered by that test, so they are placeholders; dust is set low because infrared light is expected to scatter in dust.

evidence.title: A. Nefian, Structured light system detects hazards for planetary surface navigation (NASA Ames, K-REX2 rover). Laser Focus World.
evidence.supports: About 97% positive-obstacle detection (over 99% after discarding transition images). False alarms from 1.7% at night to 4.1% in the worst daytime test. 1,158 day and 1,544 night images, lit to recreate direct sunlight and shadowed craters, on terrain about like lunar regolith in brightness.

evidence.title: The Dark Side of the Crater: How Light Looks Different on the Moon (NASA Ames).
evidence.supports: Cameras lack the sensitivity to detect rocks and craters in very dark shadows; long polar shadows hide hazards; dust loses texture at some lighting angles; early stereo results are promising. The POLAR dataset has 2,500+ stereo image pairs. No detection rates are given.

evidence.title: Design of Dust-Filtering Algorithms for LiDAR Sensors Using Intensity and Range Information in Off-Road Vehicles (Sensors).
evidence.supports: Lidar performance degrades in dust and can cause perception failures. Read as a direction only; no percentages used.

evidence.title: Why Dust Is One of the Most Complex Problems in Off-Highway Autonomy (Visage Technologies).
evidence.supports: Millimetre-wave radar shows relatively low attenuation in dust compared with optical sensing. A company article, not a measurement study, so used only for the ranking.

evidence.title: CraterGrader: Autonomous Robotic Terrain Manipulation for Lunar Site Preparation and Earthmoving (arXiv 2311.01697).
evidence.supports: Chose passive stereo because infrared scattering is expected in dusty terrain. Taken from a search summary and not read in full, so this is why the structured-light dust value is low; please verify before relying on it.

evidence.title: NASA lighting study for driving at the lunar south pole (NTRS 20240011393).
evidence.supports: At the south pole the Sun is about 1 to 2 degrees above the horizon (8 to 50 degrees during Apollo), giving long shadows and high contrast that can seriously affect safe driving.

evidence.title: VIPER mobility hardware, LSIC 2024 panel (NASA, NTRS 20240013903).
evidence.supports: VIPER carries eight LED-array lights tuned for permanently shadowed regions, with headlights for long-range stereo imaging. Used for the idea of the headlights sensor; no numbers taken.

evidence.title: ISRU Pilot Excavator (IPEx) test facility (NASA, NTRS 20250000128).
evidence.supports: NASA tests an autonomous lunar excavator under simulated south pole lighting, using onboard cameras for localisation and hazard detection. This is the kind of robot the scenario is about.

problem: Robots near the Moon's south pole must drive themselves: a radio signal to Earth and back takes time, and people can't watch every metre.
The Sun is only 1 to 2 degrees above the horizon there (8 to 50 degrees during Apollo), so rocks hide in long, black shadows.
If a robot misses a rock, it can break a wheel or tip over, and nobody can fix it.
route_note: Route challenges: a light scout rover with a camera, a stereo camera and headlights. Battery numbers are illustrative. The idea is real: at the lunar south pole the Sun circles low around the horizon, so shadows sweep across the ground, and VIPER's team planned routes to stay in sunlight because the rover is solar powered.

routes.title: Plan the route
routes.intro: A light scout rover must reach the dig site. Its sensors can't see rocks in digging dust, and its battery drains in shadow and dark craters because the solar panels only charge in sunlight. Click squares to plan a path, then drive.
routes.lesson: Plan around what the sensors can't see, and stay in the sunlight to keep the battery up.

routes.title: Moving shadows
routes.intro: At the Moon's south pole the Sun circles low around the horizon, so the shadows sweep across the ground. The battery is almost flat. Wait in the sunlight to charge, and cross when the shadow has moved.
routes.lesson: Timing matters: wait in the light for the shadows to move, instead of driving into the dark.
